question: The manual says studies show most crash-involved riders make which braking error?
choice_a: They overbrake the front tire and underbrake the rear
choice_b: They underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear
choice_c: They apply both brakes exactly equally, which is unsafe
choice_d: They never use the rear brake at all
explanation: Studies show that most crash-involved riders underbrake the front tire and overbrake the rear, or did not separate braking from swerving or choose swerving when it was appropriate.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.23, 'Crash Avoidance'

question: To stop quickly, the manual says you should squeeze the front brake lever:
choice_a: As hard and suddenly as possible
choice_b: Only after the rear brake is already locked
choice_c: Barely at all, relying mainly on the rear brake
choice_d: Firmly and progressively, without grabbing it
explanation: To stop quickly, apply both brakes at the same time. Don't be shy about using the front brake, but don't 'grab' it -- squeeze the brake lever firmly and progressively.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.23, 'Quick Stops'

question: If the front wheel locks during a quick stop, the manual instructs you to:
choice_a: Release the front brake immediately, then reapply it firmly
choice_b: Keep the front brake locked until you stop completely
choice_c: Release both brakes and coast to a stop
choice_d: Immediately apply full rear brake only
explanation: If the front wheel locks, release the front brake immediately then reapply it firmly. At the same time, press down on the rear brake.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.23, 'Quick Stops'

question: If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, the manual says you should:
choice_a: Release it immediately to avoid a skid
choice_c: Keep it locked until you have completely stopped
explanation: If you accidentally lock the rear brake on a good traction surface, keep it locked until you have completely stopped. Even with a locked rear wheel, you can control the motorcycle on a straightaway if it is upright and going straight.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.23-24, 'Quick Stops'

question: If you must stop quickly while turning or riding a curve, the manual's best technique is to:
choice_a: Brake hard while fully leaned, then straighten up
choice_b: Straighten the motorcycle upright first, then brake
choice_c: Use the rear brake only while leaned
choice_d: Continue the turn and brake at the same lean angle throughout
explanation: If you must stop quickly while turning or riding a curve, the best technique is to straighten the motorcycle upright first and then brake; if that isn't possible, apply light brakes and reduce the throttle while leaned.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.24, 'Quick Stops'

question: A swerve, as defined by the manual, is:
choice_a: Only a gradual lane change over several seconds
choice_b: A maneuver that always requires braking at the same time
choice_c: Only used when riding above the speed limit
choice_d: Any sudden change in direction, such as two quick turns or a rapid shift to the side
explanation: A swerve is any sudden change in direction. It can be two quick turns, or a rapid shift to the side.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.24, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: The manual's most important rule about combining braking and swerving is:
choice_a: Separate them -- brake before or after, never while swerving
choice_b: Always brake and swerve at the exact same instant
choice_c: Only swerve; never brake in an emergency
choice_d: Brake with the rear brake while swerving with the front
explanation: If braking is required, separate it from swerving. Brake before or after -- never while swerving.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.24, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: While swerving, the manual says you should keep your body upright and:
choice_a: Lean your body in the same direction as the motorcycle, exaggerating the lean
choice_c: Allow the motorcycle to lean in the direction of the turn while your knees stay against the tank
choice_d: Close your eyes briefly to focus on balance
explanation: Keep your body upright and allow the motorcycle to lean in the direction of the turn while keeping your knees against the tank and your feet solidly on the pegs.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.24-25, 'Swerving or Turning Quickly'

question: The manual identifies which of the following as a primary cause of single-vehicle motorcycle crashes?
choice_a: Motorcycles being struck from behind while stopped
choice_b: Motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn and colliding with the roadway or a fixed object
choice_c: Mechanical failure of the front brake
explanation: A primary cause of single-vehicle crashes is motorcyclists running wide in a curve or turn and colliding with the roadway or a fixed object.

question: Before entering a curve with no traffic present, the manual suggests starting at the outside of the curve because it:
choice_a: Is required by law on all curves
choice_b: Keeps you closer to oncoming traffic for visibility
choice_c: Reduces the need to look through the turn
choice_d: Increases your line of sight and the effective radius of the turn
explanation: If no traffic is present, start at the outside of a curve to increase your line of sight and the effective radius of the turn; as you turn, move toward the inside, and as you pass the center, move to the outside to exit.
